query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (approximately 0.1 at.%) of boron to an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy will precipitate (Hf, Zr)B2 borides preferentially at grain boundaries, thereby enhancing grain-boundary cohesion and increasing ductility and uniform deformability without a significant loss in yield strength or impact-induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA with a homogeneous BCC solid-solution matrix exhibiting intergranular brittleness and limited ductility (e.g., fracture strain ~12-13%, ultimate compressive strength ~1.75 GPa as baseline).
generation.intervention: Introduce 0.1 at.% boron during vacuum-arc melting and subsequent casting to promote intergranular boride precipitation.
generation.conditions: Tested under both quasi-static and dynamic compression (strain rates from 10^-3 s^-1 up to 3000 s^-1) at ambient temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, intergranular (Hf, Zr)B2 borides that strengthen the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion prevents intergranular crack initiation and propagation; the boride precipitation reinforces the boundaries without altering the matrix’s solid-solution strength, thereby preserving the alloy’s energy release capacity under impact.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in fracture strain (targeting ~19% ductility) and improved work hardening while maintaining yield strength near or above 1.6 GPa and exhibiting comparable impact-induced energy-release characteristics relative to the untreated baseline.
generation.baseline: Untreated HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy with ~12-13% fracture strain and ultimate compressive strength ~1.75 GPa.
generation.boundary: Ambient temperature tests under both quasi-static and high strain rate dynamic loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate; while boron-induced grain-boundary strengthening is well supported, subtle effects on reaction kinetics for energy release during impact need verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA – one with 0.1 at.% boron addition and one control. Perform compressive tests at quasi-static and dynamic strain rates, measure fracture strain, yield strength, and conduct impact tests to record energy-release characteristics.
measurements: Yield and ultimate strength under compression
High-speed imaging and energy release quantification during impact tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in fracture strain (e.g., does not reach ~19% versus ~12-13% in control) or if there is a significant degradation in yield strength or impact-induced energy release relative to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

The minor addition of boron effectively improved the mechanical properties of the alloy, as presented in the macro-compressive stress–strain curves and fractographies of the RHEA and RHEA-B samples in Figure 7, and as the yield stresses, ultimate strengths, fracture strains and work hardening percentages listed in Table 4. While the yield stress only slightly increased from 1.57 GPa for the RHEA (close to the value obtained by the above micropillar compression, 1.51 GPa) to 1.61 GPa for the RHEA-B, the work hardenability and ductility were more obviously improved. The ultimate compressive strength of the RHEA, 1.75 GPa at a fracture stain of 12.3%, showed a similarly low hardenability (for only about 11%) and ductility to typical refractory alloys. In comparison, The RHEA-B exhibited a much higher ultimate compressive strength of 2.05 GPa (hardening for 27%) and fracture stain up to 19.3%. An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was developed in this study, and the addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%, RHEA-B) further overcame the grain-boundary brittleness. As indicated by the microstructural observations and chemical analyses, a simple BCC-phase, solid-solution structure was formed in the matrices of both the alloys. The addition of boron did not obviously increase the hardness of the matrix but induced the intergranular precipitation of the HCP-phase (Hf, Zr)B2 borides which markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Attributable to the lattice distortions caused by the random distribution of different constituent elements, a diminished anisotropy in the mechanical properties was noticed, and the deformation behavior was mediated by many small slips on multiple {110} planes. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion with the addition of boron and the intergranular precipitation of borides, the work hardenability and ductility of the alloy were effectively improved, and the failure mode obviously changed from a mainly intergranular facture to a major portion of the transgranular fracture.

papers.title: Effects of Cerium Doping on the Mechanical Properties and Energy-Releasing Behavior of High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.approach: Cerium doping via vacuum-arc melting with varying Ce-content (5–25 at.%) to modulate energy-release and mechanical properties.
papers.findings: Cerium doping improved the energy-releasing characteristics (shorter delay and more violent reaction under impact), while the dynamic compressive strength trends downward with increased Ce content. The alloy showed a transition in microstructural characteristics with Ce-rich FCC regions appearing.
papers.mechanism: The hypothesis is that chemically active cerium produces large lattice distortions and modifies element segregation, which enhances reaction kinetics. However, the softening effect of Ce may reduce strength through a trade-off between dislocation pinning and solid solution strengthening.

papers.title: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Addition of a minor amount (0.1 at.%) of boron to promote the precipitation of (Hf, Zr)B2 borides at the grain boundaries.
papers.findings: The introduction of boron did not significantly alter matrix hardness, but prominently enhanced grain-boundary cohesion. This switched the fracture mode from intergranular to predominantly transgranular fracture, increased work hardenability, improved ductility, and raised the ultimate compressive strength from 1.75 GPa to 2.05 GPa with improved strain to fracture.
papers.mechanism: Boron-induced intergranular precipitation of borides reinforces grain boundaries, thereby mitigating grain-boundary brittleness. This enhanced cohesion improves uniform deformability without a major sacrifice in strength.

papers.title: Ultra-strong tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy via stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations.
papers.approach: Stepwise thermo-mechanical processing to induce a sequence of coherent nanoprecipitates (δ-lamellae and γ″ particles) within a dual-phase (BCC and FCC) matrix.
papers.findings: The alloy achieved ultrahigh yield strength (exceeding 2 GPa) with around 15% tensile ductility at ambient temperature; it also retained high strength at elevated temperatures (above 1 GPa at 800 °C).
papers.mechanism: Coherent interfaces of both the δ-lamellae and γ″ particles obstruct dislocation motion via precipitate shearing and lattice misfit strengthening while maintaining ductility because the interfaces remain coherent and do not act as crack initiation sites.

papers.title: Microstructural Design for Improving Ductility of An Initially Brittle Refractory High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Refractory high-entropy alloys (e.g., Ta0.5HfZrTi and HfNb0.18Ta0.18Ti1.27Zr systems)
papers.approach: Metastability-engineering via controlled thermal treatments to induce strain-driven phase transformations in a TRIP-like approach.
papers.findings: By promoting the formation of ductile phases (HCP or martensitic phases) locally during deformation, the alloy’s tensile ductility improves, thereby delaying strain localization and necking in alloys that were initially brittle.
papers.mechanism: The strain-induced phase transformation (akin to TRIP in steels) increases work-hardening capability by introducing a secondary, stronger phase in high-strain regions, thus retarding strain localization and premature failure.

papers.title: Synergistic Strength-Ductility Improvement in an Additively Manufactured Body-Centered Cubic HfNbTaTiZr High-Entropy Alloy via Deep Cryogenic Treatment
papers.system: HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy produced via additive manufacturing
papers.approach: Deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) to modify internal residual stresses and induce phase precipitation (formation of Ti/Zr-rich HCP precipitates) at grain boundaries.
papers.findings: DCT results in significant residual compressive stress, defect evolution, and the nucleation of a precipitated phase that together enhance both the strength and ductility of the alloy.
papers.mechanism: The cryogenic treatment introduces complex stress states that promote controlled phase transformation at grain boundaries. The resulting compressive residual stress and precipitates improve the uniform deformability and delay fracture onset.

papers.title: High-Temperature Mechanical Properties of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 Refractory High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.approach: Comprehensive mechanical testing (tensile tests, cold rolling and annealing) across a wide temperature range (room temperature to >1200 K) to probe deformation behavior.
papers.findings: The alloy maintains high yield strength (above 800–1000 MPa, depending on temperature) with stable ductility characteristics at both ambient and elevated temperatures, indicating excellent performance under dynamic loading.
papers.mechanism: Solid-solution strengthening combined with stable dislocation slip accounts for the excellent high-temperature performance, although the dynamic interplay of grain structure and elemental interactions remains complex.

papers.title: Achieving Excellent Strength-Ductility Balance in Single-Phase CoCrNiV Multi-Principal Element Alloy.
papers.system: CoCrNiV single-phase FCC multi-principal element alloy
papers.approach: Rolling and annealing treatments to achieve a fine-grained structure with controlled grain size and solid solution strengthening via vanadium addition.
papers.findings: The CoCrNiV alloy attains a high yield strength (>1 GPa) and uniform elongation (around 24%), demonstrating a beneficial balance between strength and ductility.
papers.mechanism: Fine grain strengthening combined with lattice distortions from vanadium addition enhances strain-hardening capability via dislocation slip and the formation of stacking faults, contributing to uniform deformability.

established: Minor elemental additions (such as boron) can enhance grain-boundary cohesion and change fracture modes from intergranular to transgranular.
Controlled nanoprecipitation strategies (e.g., via stepwise thermo-mechanical processing) can achieve simultaneous high strength and improved ductility.
Microstructure and phase distribution–including grain size, precipitate type, and phase stability–are critical determinants of ductility and impact energy release in refractory HEAs.
Metastability-engineering approaches (akin to TRIP mechanisms) can be used to improve ductility in otherwise brittle refractory HEAs.

approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced energetic behavior (faster, more violent energy release) but with a reduction in dynamic compressive strength; trade-offs exist between softening and dislocation pinning effects.
Marked improvement in ductility and work hardenability with minimal changes to yield strength, achieved via enhanced grain-boundary cohesion.
Simultaneously achieved ultrahigh strength and adequate ductility; effective at ambient and elevated temperatures.
Enhanced strength and ductility through the induction of residual compressive stresses and controlled phase precipitation.
Improved tensile ductility in initially brittle RHEAs by promoting ductile phase formation and delaying strain localization.

approaches_tried.approach: Grain refinement through rolling and annealing
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced strength and ductility balance in single-phase alloys, achieved via fine grain strengthening and solid solution effects.

mechanisms: Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion through precipitation (as with boron-induced (Hf, Zr)B2 formation).
Dual-phase strengthening via coherent nanoprecipitates that hinder dislocation motion without compromising ductility.
Residual compressive stress and controlled phase precipitation induced by deep cryogenic treatment.
Strain-induced phase transformations (metastability-engineering) that promote TRIP-like effects to delay necking.
disagreements: Cerium doping shows promising energy-release improvements but at the apparent cost of reduced strength and potentially compromised ductility, leaving uncertainties over its net benefit.

There is debate over the optimal balance between precipitation strengthening (which tends to increase strength) and the need to maintain sufficient ductility and uniform deformability in energetic structural applications.
open_questions: How can ductility and uniform deformability be improved in RHEAs for energetic structural materials without sacrificing high strength and impact-induced energy release?
What is the optimal combination or sequence of interventions (e.g., boron addition, nanoprecipitation control, cryogenic treatment) that delivers synergistic improvements?
How robust are these interventions under dynamic, high-strain-rate conditions typical of energetic structural applications?
opportunities: Investigate a hybrid approach combining minor boron addition with controlled, stepwise coherent nanoprecipitation to enhance grain-boundary cohesion while maintaining or boosting strength and energy release.
Explore the synergy between deep cryogenic treatment and precipitation engineering to tune residual stresses and phase distributions in RHEAs.

Conduct systematic studies under dynamic loading (including impact tests) to validate whether these microstructural interventions can deliver improved ductility and uniform deformability without degrading energetic performance.

directions.direction: Minor elemental addition of a grain‐boundary strengthening element (e.g. boron) to promote intergranular precipitation of borides.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses grain‐boundary brittleness by enhancing cohesion without significantly softening the matrix. Strong supporting evidence from boron‐doped RHEAs (e.g. PMC9572892) makes this a feasible and testable approach.

directions.direction: Stepwise thermo‐mechanical processing to induce dual coherent nanoprecipitations (δ‐lamellae and γ″ particles) in a tungsten-based HEA.
directions.assessment: The sequential formation of coherent nano-precipitates has been shown to achieve ultrahigh strength with improved ductility (PMC10213035) and can be tuned to preserve high-impact energy release. However, slight process deviations might affect the energy-release kinetics.

directions.direction: Deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) to induce residual compressive stresses and controlled grain-boundary phase precipitation in additively manufactured RHEAs.
directions.assessment: Cryogenic treatment has been demonstrated to generate beneficial residual stress and precipitate formation (PMC11355962), enhancing ductility while retaining strength. Feasible under controlled conditions and directly testable under dynamic loading.

directions.direction: Metastability engineering via controlled annealing to produce a matrix that undergoes TRIP-like strain-induced transformation.
directions.assessment: Strain-induced transformation (TRIP effect) can delay necking and improve uniform deformability (PMC5995863). The intervention is conceptually attractive but its impact on energetic release must be carefully verified to ensure no detrimental softening.

directions.direction: Surface treatments or coatings that modify friction and stress distribution at microstructural level.
directions.assessment: While potentially beneficial for uniform deformation, surface approaches may not address the bulk material’s intrinsic ductility and are less directly related to maintaining energy release under impact conditions.

candidates.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (approximately 0.1 at.%) of boron to an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy will precipitate (Hf, Zr)B2 borides preferentially at grain boundaries, thereby enhancing grain-boundary cohesion and increasing ductility and uniform deformability without a significant loss in yield strength or impact-induced energy release.
candidates.intervention: Introduce 0.1 at.% boron during vacuum-arc melting and subsequent casting to promote intergranular boride precipitation.

candidates.hypothesis: A two-step thermo‐mechanical aging treatment in a tungsten‐based refractory HEA—first, aging at approximately 1050°C for 30 minutes to nucleate fine δ‐lamellar precipitates, followed by quenching and a second aging at about 750°C for 45 minutes to form coherent 10 nm γ″ precipitates—will synergistically enhance ductility and uniform deformability while preserving high yield strength and dynamic impact-induced energy release.
candidates.intervention: Apply the two‐step aging treatment with the following protocol: heat to 1050°C for 30 minutes to induce δ‐lamellar precipitates, quench rapidly to room temperature, then reheat to 750°C for 45 minutes to precipitate coherent γ″ particles.
candidates.changes: Added specific treatment parameters to improve reproducibility and clarity. Detailed the two-step aging process with defined temperature and time windows to address reviewer concerns regarding process control and the impact on energetic performance.

candidates.hypothesis: A controlled slow-cooling annealing treatment that creates a metastable BCC matrix in a Ta0.5HfZrTi refractory HEA—specifically, furnace annealing at 950°C for 2 hours followed by a slow cooling at 0.1°C/min—will promote a strain-induced transformation (TRIP effect) during deformation, thereby enhancing ductility and uniform deformability without compromising high yield strength or impact-induced energy release.
candidates.intervention: Subject the alloy to furnace annealing at 950°C for 2 hours, then cool very slowly at 0.1°C/min to room temperature to achieve a metastable BCC matrix.
candidates.changes: Specified detailed annealing parameters to ensure reproducibility and incorporated explicit temperature and cooling rate to generate the required metastable BCC state for TRIP-like transformation. Reinforced the connection to previous studies on strain-induced transformation in refractory HEAs.

candidates.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (approximately 0.1 at.%) of boron to an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy will induce the preferential precipitation of (Hf, Zr)B₂ borides at grain boundaries, thereby enhancing grain-boundary cohesion and increasing ductility and uniform deformability without significantly reducing yield strength or impacting the material’s high dynamic energy release under impact.
candidates.intervention: Incorporate 0.1 at.% boron during vacuum-arc melting and casting to promote controlled intergranular precipitation of (Hf, Zr)B₂ borides.
candidates.changes: Clarified processing conditions and confirmed that boron addition is carried out under controlled casting conditions. Emphasized validation of boride morphology and uniformity through high-resolution compositional mapping to address reviewer concerns about reproducibility and its impact on energetic behavior.

candidates.hypothesis: Deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) of an additively manufactured HfNbTaTiZr refractory HEA—by soaking in liquid nitrogen at approximately -196°C for 48 hours followed by controlled reheat at 5°C/min—will induce the formation of a Ti/Zr-rich HCP phase at grain boundaries and generate beneficial residual compressive stresses, thereby improving ductility and deformation uniformity without sacrificing high yield strength or impact-induced energy release.
candidates.intervention: Subject the alloy to deep cryogenic treatment by immersing in liquid nitrogen (-196°C) for 48 hours, then reheat to room temperature at a controlled rate of 5°C/min.
candidates.changes: Adjusted the deep cryogenic treatment duration from 120 hours to a more practical 48 hours and specified a controlled reheat protocol to improve industrial scalability and reproducibility. Provided clearer details on the processing parameters and microstructural assessment.

minor_issues: Uncertain whether the proposed slow-cooling route consistently yields the requisite metastability to trigger TRIP in dynamic conditions.
Limited direct evidence linking the proposed microstructural transformations to high strain-rate (energetic) behavior.
fixes: Include thorough in-situ high strain rate testing (e.g., Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar) with diffraction-based or in-situ microscopy confirmation of the strain-induced transformation.
Demonstrate microstructural stability and TRIP activation under relevant loading rates and temperatures.
evidence_needs: Phase stability diagrams or time–temperature–transformation data for Ta0.5HfZrTi under slow-cooling conditions.
Comparative data showing uniform elongation and strength retention at both quasi-static and dynamic strain rates to confirm the TRIP-induced improvements.

minor_issues: Mechanism of Ti/Zr-rich HCP phase formation and its stability under rapid loading remains less established for DCT in refractory HEAs compared to more conventional alloys.
Unclear whether the 48-hour deep cryogenic treatment provides robust or reproducible microstructural changes for industrial-scale components.
fixes: Perform detailed microstructural characterization (TEM, XRD) before, during, and after DCT to confirm the formation of HCP precipitates and residual stresses.
Investigate the effect of varying cryogenic soak time and reheat rate on microstructure and mechanical properties to optimize the treatment protocol.
evidence_needs: Experimental validation of residual stress magnitude and distribution via diffraction-based stress measurements before and after DCT.
Side-by-side dynamic compression or impact-energy comparisons of DCT-treated versus untreated samples to confirm no loss of energetic performance.

minor_issues: Limited explicit discussion of high-rate impact or energetic testing results, although references suggest potential preservation of dynamic performance.
fixes: Design and report high-strain-rate or dynamic impact tests to confirm that the added boron does not adversely affect energy release or cause embrittlement at faster loading rates.
evidence_needs: In-situ or post-mortem microstructural analysis of grain-boundary boride phases under dynamic loading to confirm their integrity under shock conditions.
Quantitative correlation between (Hf, Zr)B2 precipitate distribution, grain size, and mechanical response at high strain rates.

major_issues: Substantially duplicates the approach of Candidate C with minimal distinction in mechanism or scope.
minor_issues: Novelty relative to Candidate C is unclear; no new microstructural insight or processing distinction beyond what is already proposed.
fixes: Clarify the unique aspects—if any—beyond the introduction of 0.1 at.% boron that differentiate this hypothesis from Candidate C.
Provide additional mechanistic details or alternative characterization routes to distinguish it from existing boron-doped RHEA approaches.
evidence_needs: Same as Candidate C: direct mechanical tests under dynamic loading, thorough microstructural characterization, and demonstration of energetic performance.

minor_issues: Claimed significant increase in yield strength (from ~600 MPa to ~2.0 GPa) is high; evidence that the second aging step preserves or enhances energetic performance is not clearly demonstrated.
Insufficient detail on how the δ-lamellar and γ″ precipitates behave at high strain rates and under impact loading.
fixes: Provide robust characterization (TEM, atom probe) to confirm the presence and stability of both δ and γ″ phases and their role in high-strain-rate deformation.
Add direct impact or ballistic tests to validate that the dual-precipitation mechanism does not degrade the material’s energetic release characteristics.
evidence_needs: Detailed time–temperature–precipitation data for tungsten-based HEAs showing the formation and stability of δ and γ″ phases.

Verification from dynamic mechanical tests (e.g., split-Hopkinson bar experiments) linking the precipitation microstructure to both high strength and retained ductility in the high-strain-rate regime.

minor_issues: The hypothesis could benefit from a more detailed discussion of potential trade-offs between boride precipitation and dynamic energy release.
fixes: Include a discussion of how boride precipitation might affect impact-induced energy release mechanisms.
evidence_needs: Further experimental data on the dynamic energy release behavior of boron-doped RHEAs under high strain rates.

major_issues: The mechanism of residual stress generation and its interaction with grain-boundary strengthening is not fully explained.
minor_issues: The hypothesis does not specify how the Ti/Zr-rich HCP phase will affect dynamic energy release.
fixes: Clarify the role of residual stresses and HCP phase formation in enhancing ductility and maintaining impact energy release.
evidence_needs: Experimental validation of the formation of the Ti/Zr-rich HCP phase and its effect on mechanical properties.

minor_issues: The hypothesis could elaborate on the potential effects of boride size and distribution on mechanical properties.
fixes: Provide a more detailed discussion of how boride size and distribution influence the predicted outcomes.
evidence_needs: Additional data on the relationship between boride morphology and mechanical properties in similar RHEAs.

major_issues: The hypothesis does not sufficiently address the potential impact of the two-step aging treatment on dynamic energy release.
minor_issues: The proposed aging parameters may require further optimization to ensure reproducibility.
fixes: Include a discussion of how the two-step aging treatment affects dynamic energy release and propose additional experiments to optimize aging parameters.
evidence_needs: Experimental data on the impact of the two-step aging treatment on dynamic energy release.

major_issues: The hypothesis assumes that the TRIP effect will occur under dynamic conditions without direct evidence.
minor_issues: The slow-cooling rate may introduce practical challenges in scaling up the process for industrial applications.
fixes: Provide a more detailed explanation of how the TRIP effect will manifest under dynamic conditions and address potential scalability issues.
evidence_needs: Experimental validation of the TRIP effect under high strain rates in Ta0.5HfZrTi RHEAs.

minor_issues: The hypothesis could benefit from more detailed explanation of how the δ-lamellar and γ″ precipitates interact with dislocations to enhance ductility and strength.
fixes: Provide additional theoretical or experimental evidence to support the proposed mechanism of δ-lamellar and γ″ precipitate interaction with dislocations.
evidence_needs: Further studies on the effects of varying the aging treatment parameters on the precipitate morphology and mechanical properties would be beneficial.

minor_issues: The TRIP effect's influence on dynamic impact-induced energy release is less documented and requires more experimental verification.
fixes: Conduct additional experiments to investigate the TRIP effect under high-strain-rate conditions and its impact on energy release.
evidence_needs: More research is needed to understand the strain-induced phase transformation's effect on the alloy's behavior under dynamic loading.
Investigating the effects of boron addition on the alloy's microstructure and mechanical properties under various testing conditions would provide further insight.
Further research on the optimal boron content and its influence on the mechanical properties and microstructure would be beneficial.

minor_issues: The exact mechanism by which DCT induces the formation of a Ti/Zr-rich HCP phase and beneficial residual stresses needs further clarification.
fixes: Provide more detailed theoretical or experimental analysis of the DCT process's effects on the microstructure and residual stresses.
evidence_needs: Additional studies on the effects of varying the DCT parameters on the resulting microstructure and mechanical properties would be valuable.
